b: A hundred and fifty prayers and songs, collected into five books, covering the entire emotional range. Roughly a third are laments — complaints, protests and demands — which is more than any other kind. God put a book of complaints inside his own book.
Jesus prayed these, quoted them constantly, and died with one on his lips. If you do not know what to pray, start here rather than trying to invent something.

1.t: Two ways, two ends. Placed first deliberately: the whole collection is to be read as instruction, not only as prayer.

2.t: A royal psalm quoted more in the New Testament than almost any other. Verse 7 is spoken at Jesus' baptism and transfiguration.

8.t: Opens and closes with the same line. Hebrews 2 applies the middle of it to Christ.
The question arises from looking at the sky, not from introspection. Hebrews 2 applies the answer to Christ.

16.h: You will not abandon me to Sheol
16.t: Peter quotes this at Pentecost, arguing that David spoke it of the Messiah because David's own tomb was still there.
In your presence is fullness of joy. Peter quotes verses 8 to 11 at Pentecost.

19.t: Creation speaks without words; the law speaks with them. The psalm moves from the sky to Scripture to the psalmist's own hidden faults.

19.h: Let the words of my mouth
19.t: The prayer that many preachers still use before speaking, and it comes at the end of a psalm about the heavens and the law.

22.t: The line Jesus quotes from the cross. The psalm describes pierced hands and feet, divided garments and casting lots, then turns at verse 22 to vindication and worldwide worship.
Written centuries before crucifixion was practised. Bones out of joint, a tongue stuck to the jaw, garments divided by lot — all quoted at the cross.

23.t: The most familiar psalm in the world, and note that the valley is walked through rather than avoided, and that the table is set in the presence of enemies rather than after their defeat.
Not around it, and the pronouns change here from 'he' to 'you'. The psalmist stops describing God and starts speaking to him.

32.t: Paul quotes this in Romans 4 as evidence of righteousness credited apart from works. Verses 3 and 4 describe the physical effects of unconfessed sin with unusual precision.
God speaking in the middle of a psalm about confession. Forgiveness leads to guidance, in that order.

42.t: Thirst as the image for longing. The psalmist's tears have been his food and he preaches to his own soul.
The psalmist talks to himself rather than merely listening to himself, which is the practical move the psalm teaches.

46.t: Though the earth give way and the mountains fall into the sea. The refuge is named before the crisis is described.

Often read as an invitation to quiet reflection; in context it is closer to 'stop' — addressed to raging nations, not to anxious individuals. It comforts for a different reason than people usually think.

51.t: The model penitential psalm. Note verse 4 — against you only have I sinned — and that what God is said to want is a broken spirit rather than sacrifice.

51.h: Create in me a pure heart
51.t: The verb is the one used in Genesis 1 for creating out of nothing. David is not asking for repair.

73.t: The most honest treatment of envy in Scripture. The psalmist nearly loses his footing over the prosperity of the wicked, and what changes is not his circumstances but his vantage point.

73.h: Whom have I in heaven but you
73.t: My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart. Written by a man who had almost lost his footing.

90.t: From everlasting to everlasting you are God. Moses' psalm opens with permanence before describing how short life is.

90.h: Teach us to number our days
90.t: Attributed to Moses, the oldest psalm in the collection, and the only sensible response to its own bleak arithmetic.

103.h: Bless the LORD, O my soul
103.t: A catalogue of benefits, and then verse 14 — he remembers that we are dust. The tenderness of that is easy to miss.

103.h: As far as the east is from the west
103.t: A distance with no measure, unlike north and south which meet at the poles.

110.h: The LORD said to my Lord
110.t: The most frequently quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament. Jesus uses it himself to press the question of how the Messiah can be both David's son and David's Lord.
In the order of Melchizedek. Hebrews builds several chapters on this half-verse.

119.t: An acrostic of twenty-two stanzas of eight verses, each stanza beginning with a successive Hebrew letter. Almost every verse mentions God's word under one of eight terms. The form is a discipline, not decoration.
Enough light for the next step rather than the whole road, which is how guidance usually arrives.

130.t: With you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared — not that you may be taken lightly. Forgiveness produces reverence rather than casualness.
My soul waits for the Lord. Luther called this one of the Pauline psalms.

139.t: Omniscience, omnipresence and creation applied personally rather than abstractly. It ends by inviting the searching it began by describing.

139.h: Knit together in my mother's womb
139.t: All my days were written before one of them came to be.

150.t: The Psalter has run through lament, protest, doubt and despair, and it ends in unqualified praise. The order is the argument.

3.t: The superscription places this during Absalom's rebellion. He lies down and sleeps anyway.

6.t: Worn out from groaning, drenching the bed with tears. Scripture does not require composure.

13.t: Four 'how longs', then two requests, then trust. The shape of nearly every lament, in six verses.

27.t: Confidence and fear side by side in one psalm. It ends with wait for the LORD, repeated, which suggests nothing had yet resolved.

34.t: That the LORD is good. Peter quotes this psalm in his first letter.
And he saves the crushed in spirit. Verse 8 — taste and see — comes from the same psalm.

37.t: Three times. The counsel is to trust, delight, commit and be still, which is harder than it reads.

40.t: He put a new song in my mouth. Paul's language about rescue has this psalm behind it.

63.t: Written in the wilderness. Your love is better than life — an extraordinary sentence from a man with no water.

84.t: A pilgrim psalm. The valley of weeping becomes a place of springs for those passing through it.

84.h: Better one day in your courts
84.t: Than a thousand elsewhere. The psalmist would rather be a doorkeeper.

88.h: The one that does not turn
88.t: Almost alone among the laments, this one never resolves. It ends in darkness. God left it in, which is the most pastorally useful fact about it.

91.h: He who dwells in the shelter
91.t: Quoted by Satan at the temptation, which is a caution about lifting promises out of context.

100.h: Know that the LORD is God
100.t: Seven imperatives in five verses. It is we who are his, and not we ourselves who made us.

116.t: Because he heard. A thanksgiving psalm after deliverance from death, with the honest admission in verse 11 that he said in his alarm that everyone is a liar.

121.t: A song of ascents, sung going up to Jerusalem. He who watches over you will not slumber — said six times in eight verses.

127.t: Work without God is described as anxious toil. The second half gives sleep to those he loves.

133.t: Three verses on the good of brotherhood, pictured as oil running down Aaron's beard.

145.t: The LORD is good to all, and his compassion is over all he has made. An acrostic psalm of praise.

15.t: A short catalogue of ordinary integrity — keeping an oath even when it hurts, lending without interest.

25.t: An acrostic psalm of guidance, with the admission in verse 16 that he is lonely and afflicted.

30.h: Weeping may stay for the night
30.t: Rejoicing comes in the morning. Written for the dedication of the temple and still used at funerals.

33.h: By the word of the LORD
33.t: The heavens were made. Creation by speech, picked up in John 1 and Hebrews 11.
Whose God is the LORD. Often applied to modern countries; written about the people God chose.

62.t: Repeated at the start and the middle. Verse 8 — pour out your hearts to him — is the instruction the psalm is modelling.

65.t: An agricultural psalm about rain, pastures and hills clothed with gladness. Not every psalm is about crisis.

77.t: The turn of the psalm is a deliberate act of memory. He stops asking and starts recounting.

86.t: Teach me your way that I may rely on your faithfulness. One of the best short prayers in the Psalter.

95.h: Today, if you hear his voice
95.t: Quoted at length in Hebrews 3 and 4, introduced there as the Holy Spirit speaking.

96.t: Declare his glory among the nations. Missionary theology centuries before the Great Commission.

102.t: Addressed to the LORD here, and applied to the Son in Hebrews 1:10–12.

107.t: Wanderers, prisoners, the sick and sailors, each with the refrain: then they cried to the LORD in their trouble. Verse 29 — he stilled the storm — is what the disciples would have known.

115.h: Those who make idols will be like them
115.t: A sharp little argument: idols have mouths that cannot speak, and their makers become as lifeless as what they worship.

118.t: Quoted by Jesus of himself, and by Peter before the Sanhedrin. The most cited psalm verse in the New Testament after 110:1.

118.h: This is the day the LORD has made
118.t: In context, the day of an unexpected deliverance rather than any day in general.

126.t: Those who sow in tears will reap with songs of joy. A song of ascents for people returning from exile.

131.t: Three verses. The image is of a child no longer crying for what it wants, simply content to be held.

138.h: The LORD will fulfil his purpose
138.t: He will not abandon the works of his hands. Confidence grounded in God's character rather than circumstances.

143.t: Word of your unfailing love, for I have put my trust in you. A psalm for starting the day badly.

146.h: Do not put your trust in princes
146.t: Their plans come to nothing on the day they die. A necessary corrective in every generation.

4.h: In peace I will lie down
4.t: You alone make me dwell in safety. An evening psalm, and the companion to Psalm 3's morning.

5.h: In the morning I lay my requests
5.t: And wait expectantly. The waiting is named as part of the praying.

7.h: Bring to an end the violence
7.t: You who probe minds and hearts. Justice asked for by someone who accepts being examined himself.

9.t: Those who know your name trust in you. Knowing the name means knowing the character.

10.h: Why do you stand far off
10.t: The psalm asks it without apology and spends most of its length describing the wicked before turning.

11.t: What can the righteous do? The answer given is that the LORD is in his holy temple — a change of vantage rather than of circumstance.

12.t: Like silver refined seven times, set against the flattering lips of verse 2.

14.h: The fool says in his heart
14.t: There is no God. Paul quotes this psalm at length in Romans 3.

17.t: Hide me in the shadow of your wings. Two images of close protection in one verse.

18.t: Rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn, stronghold. Six metaphors before the psalm has properly begun.

20.t: But we trust in the name of the LORD our God. A war psalm that names the actual security.

21.t: A royal psalm, and the New Testament reads this line of psalms as pointing beyond David.

24.t: Clean hands and a pure heart. The psalm ends with the gates lifting for the King of glory.

26.t: Examine my heart and my mind. Few psalms invite scrutiny this directly.

28.t: The LORD is my strength and my shield. The turn comes at verse 6, after six verses of pleading.

29.t: Seven times, over the waters, breaking cedars, shaking the desert. A storm psalm that ends in the temple.

31.t: I commit my spirit — the words Jesus spoke from the cross.

35.t: An imprecatory psalm. Note the psalmist asks God to act rather than acting himself, which is the model. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

36.h: Your love reaches to the heavens
36.t: In your light we see light. The psalm moves from the wickedness of sin to the breadth of God's love in three verses.

38.t: Physical description of guilt — no soundness in my body, wounds festering. The body keeps the account.

39.h: Show me the measure of my days
39.t: Let me know how fleeting my life is. Honest about mortality in a way modern religion rarely is.

41.t: Has lifted up his heel against me. Jesus quotes it of Judas.

43.t: The continuation of Psalm 42; the two were probably one psalm. The refrain closes both.

44.t: Why do you sleep? A communal lament that accuses God of forgetting, and it is in Scripture.

45.t: A wedding psalm for a king, quoted in Hebrews 1 and applied to the Son.

47.t: God reigns over the nations — one of the psalms that refuses to keep God local.

48.h: This God is our God for ever
48.t: He will be our guide even to the end. The psalm walks round Jerusalem's walls and towers, then concludes that the real security was never the fortifications but the God who dwells there.

49.t: When someone grows rich, for they will take nothing with them. Ecclesiastes in miniature.

50.h: The cattle on a thousand hills
50.t: God says that if he were hungry he would not tell us. An argument against thinking worship supplies him something.

52.t: Flourishing in the house of God, set against the man who trusted in his wealth.

53.t: With minor variations. The Psalter preserves both, which tells you something about how it was assembled.

55.h: If an enemy were insulting me
55.t: But it is you, a man like myself, my companion. Betrayal by a friend, described precisely.

56.h: You keep track of my sorrows
56.t: Record my misery, list my tears on your scroll. An extraordinary image of being noticed.

57.h: In the shadow of your wings
57.t: Until the disaster has passed. Written in a cave, according to the superscription.

59.h: I will sing of your strength
59.t: In the morning I will sing of your love, for you are my fortress. Written while his house was being watched.

61.h: The rock that is higher than I
61.t: Lead me to it — an admission that he cannot get there himself.

66.h: If I had cherished sin in my heart
66.t: The Lord would not have listened. A sobering verse about unanswered prayer.

67.h: That your ways may be known
67.t: The blessing asked for is so that it reaches the nations. Mission built into a benediction.

68.t: God sets the lonely in families. Paul quotes verse 18 in Ephesians 4.

69.t: Quoted by the disciples when Jesus cleared the temple. The psalm is quoted in the New Testament more than most.

71.h: Do not cast me away when I am old
71.t: A psalm of a man past his strength, still asking to declare God's power to the next generation.

72.h: A king who defends the afflicted
72.t: Solomon's psalm, and the standard by which every later king was measured and found wanting.

75.t: No one from the east or west can exalt a man; God brings one down and lifts another up.

78.t: A long retelling of Israel's history so that children would put their trust in God and not forget.

80.t: Make your face shine on us. The refrain appears three times, each time more urgent.

81.t: And I will fill it — followed by the lament that Israel would not listen.

85.t: Righteousness and peace kiss each other. Four attributes personified in one line.

89.h: I will sing of the LORD's great love
89.t: A psalm about the covenant with David that ends, forty verses later, asking where that love has gone.

92.h: They will still bear fruit in old age
92.t: Planted in the house of the LORD. A sabbath psalm.

93.t: Mightier than the thunder of the great waters. Four verses, all about stability.

94.h: When anxiety was great within me
94.t: Your consolation brought me joy. A verse worth knowing by heart.

97.h: Let those who love the LORD hate evil
97.t: Love and hatred held together as one instruction.

98.t: The psalm behind 'Joy to the World'. The rivers clap and the mountains sing.

99.t: The threefold 'he is holy' in this psalm anticipates Isaiah 6.

101.t: In my own house — and set no vile thing before my eyes. A psalm about private integrity.

104.t: Following the order of Genesis 1. Verse 15 mentions wine that gladdens human hearts without embarrassment.

105.t: Israel's history retold with the emphasis on God's faithfulness rather than their failure — the opposite emphasis to Psalm 106.

106.t: Same history, told as a catalogue of rebellion. The Psalter puts both versions side by side on purpose.

111.t: The beginning of wisdom. An acrostic psalm, paired with 112.

112.t: His heart is steadfast, trusting in the LORD. Not the absence of bad news, but of dread about it.

113.h: He raises the poor from the dust
113.t: Hannah's song and Mary's both draw on this psalm.

117.t: Two verses, addressed to all nations. Paul quotes it in Romans 15 as evidence the Gentiles were always in view.

120.h: I call on the LORD in my distress
120.t: The first of the fifteen songs of ascents, sung going up to Jerusalem.

122.h: I rejoiced with those who said
122.t: Let us go to the house of the LORD. A pilgrim's psalm about being glad to go.

123.t: Look to the hand of their master, so our eyes look to the LORD. Watching for a signal.

124.h: Our help is in the name of the LORD
124.t: The maker of heaven and earth. Used as an opening sentence in churches for centuries.

125.t: So the LORD surrounds his people. The geography is the argument.

128.h: Blessed are all who fear the LORD
128.t: Ordinary domestic blessing — food from your labour, a family round the table.

129.h: They have not gained the victory
129.t: A psalm of a people who have been ploughed over and are still there.

132.t: A psalm about bringing the ark to Jerusalem and about God's promise in return.

134.t: Three verses, addressed to those who minister by night in the house of the LORD.

135.h: Those who make them will be like them
135.t: The same argument as Psalm 115: you become what you worship.

136.t: Twenty-six times. Designed to be sung antiphonally, and the repetition is the point rather than a flaw.

137.t: It begins in grief and ends with a line about dashing infants on rocks. Honest rage handed to God rather than acted on.

137.h: Can a Christian pray a psalm like this
137.t: These verses are among the most shocking in the Bible. They are the honest cry of people who had watched their own children killed by Babylon, and the psalmist takes that rage to God instead of acting on it. The Psalms model bringing every emotion to God, including ones we should not act out. Christians read these psalms through the cross, where Jesus prayed for his enemies, and through God's promise that vengeance belongs to him. The appropriate response is not to pray the words against people we dislike, but to learn from them that God can bear the full weight of our anger and that justice is safe in his hands. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

140.h: The LORD secures justice for the poor
140.t: The conclusion of a psalm asking for protection from violent men.

141.h: Set a guard over my mouth
141.t: And verse 5: let a righteous man strike me, it is a kindness. A prayer to be corrected.

142.h: No one cares for my life
142.t: Written in the cave. The loneliest sentence in the Psalter.

144.h: What is mankind that you care
144.t: A fleeting breath, a passing shadow. The psalm still ends asking for blessing.

147.t: And determines the number of the stars, in consecutive verses. The Psalter refuses to separate the cosmic from the personal.

148.t: Angels, sun, sea creatures, weather, mountains, kings and children. A comprehensive summons.

149.t: Praise combined with a two-edged sword. The psalm is used carefully in Christian tradition, and should be.

54.t: Written when the Ziphites betrayed David's location to Saul. The psalm is four verses of plea and three of confidence.

58.h: Break the teeth of the wicked
58.t: An imprecatory psalm against corrupt rulers. The psalmist asks God to act rather than acting himself, and the aim is that people will say there is a God who judges. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

60.t: With God we will gain the victory. Written after a defeat.

64.t: A psalm about slander and plotting words, ending with God's arrow turning their own tongues against them.

70.t: Come quickly to me. Almost identical to the end of Psalm 40.

74.h: Why have you rejected us for ever
74.t: A lament over the destroyed temple. The psalmist reminds God of creation and of his covenant, arguing from God's own record.

76.t: Even the anger of men is turned to serve God's purposes.

79.t: Grief over Jerusalem's destruction, asking for help for the sake of God's name rather than Israel's merit.

82.t: A difficult psalm. Jesus quotes verse 6 in John 10. Interpreters divide over whether the 'gods' are human judges or heavenly beings. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

83.t: The psalm asks for the enemies to be shamed so that they will seek God's name and know he is Most High.

87.t: Egypt, Babylon, Philistia and Tyre recorded as born there. Nations counted as citizens of God's city — a startling Old Testament picture.

108.t: Parts of Psalm 57 and Psalm 60 combined into one. The Psalter reuses its own material.

109.t: A sustained curse on a false accuser. Peter applies verse 8 to Judas. Read as honest rage entrusted to God, not a pattern for our own speech. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

114.t: A short, vivid poem on the exodus. The mountains skip like rams at the presence of God.
